stories.title: Nāsadīya Sūkta
stories.subtitle: A hymn that refuses to finish the story of creation
stories.summary: Rigveda 10.129 does not tell a complete cosmogony. It asks, in order, what there was, what arose, and who could know.
stories.layerNote: This page is editorial narrative. It points to the hymn; it is not a substitute for the hymn. Later Purāṇic creation stories are a different layer of tradition and are not silently mixed in here.

blocks.text: Among the late hymns of the tenth maṇḍala is a short speculative poem often called the Nāsadīya, after its opening words. It is not a temple liturgy in the usual sense, and it is not a later Purāṇic account of Brahmā or a cosmic egg. What the hymn itself does is proceed by questions.
It begins by refusing the usual pair of being and non-being. At that time, it says, there was neither asat nor sat; there was no mid-space (rajas), nor the sky beyond. {ref:RV.10.129.1}
The opening verse is the claim most often quoted. Read it as the hymn states it, not as a later philosophy textbook.
Death is not there yet, nor deathlessness. Night and day have not been marked. Something the hymn calls “that one” (tad ekam) breathes without wind, by its own svadhā. {ref:RV.10.129.2}

Darkness is covered by darkness; the all is indistinguishable water. From the might of tapas — heat, austerity, fermentation of force — a unit is born. {ref:RV.10.129.3} Then desire (kāma) arises as the first seed of mind, and poets, searching in the heart, find a kinship of sat in asat. {ref:RV.10.129.4}
The famous turn is epistemological. Who truly knows, who can say here, from where this emission (visṛṣṭi) was born? The gods are later than this production. {ref:RV.10.129.6}
The last verse does not resolve the question with a creator’s name. The overseer in the highest sky may know — or perhaps does not know. {ref:RV.10.129.7}

Later Indian literature retells creation in many other ways: golden embryo, Puruṣa divided, Brahmā, prakṛti and puruṣa. Those are real traditions, but they are not this hymn. This library keeps them distinct. Related Rigvedic cosmogonies, with different arguments, are the Puruṣa Sūkta and the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn.

stories.title: Yama and Yamī
stories.subtitle: A dialogue concerning desire, kinship and cosmic order
stories.summary: Rigveda 10.10 is a conversation, not a later legend of the first humans. Yamī presses for union; Yama refuses on the ground of kinship and the law watched by the gods.
stories.layerNote: Editorial framing only. The hymn is a dialogue in the Rigveda. Later stories that make Yama and Yamī the first pair of humans, or that resolve the argument differently, belong to later tradition.

blocks.text: The tenth maṇḍala preserves a dialogue between Yama and Yamī. In the hymn they speak as twins. Yamī seeks a bond that would produce offspring; Yama answers that such a bond would violate a kinship the gods themselves watch. The page follows claims in the sukta. It does not complete the plot from later myth.
Yamī opens by trying to turn a friend toward friendship, and by speaking of a son who would continue the father. {ref:RV.10.10.1}
Yamī argues that their relationship should not prevent their union. The immortals, she says, desire offspring of the one mortal; she asks that mind be set in mind, husband to body. {ref:RV.10.10.3}
Yamī’s proposal is in the hymn, not in a later romance.
Yama rejects the proposal and appeals to moral and cosmic restraint. What was never done before should not be done now. {ref:RV.10.10.4}
He names the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa as great, and says the sentinels of the gods do not close their eyes. {ref:RV.10.10.6} {ref:RV.10.10.8}

Yamī speaks desire without euphemism: she would lie on the same couch, like a wife, like chariot wheels meeting. {ref:RV.10.10.7} The hymn does not convert this into a wedding, and it does not punish her. It leaves the refusal standing through the remaining verses. {ref:RV.10.10.14}

Later tradition often treats Yama as the first to die and as lord of the departed, and sometimes treats Yamī as the river Yamunā. Those identifications are historically important. They are not the plot of Ṛgveda 10.10. A different Rigvedic Yama appears in the funeral hymn, where he is addressed as king of the gathering-place of men — still not the later Purāṇic judge of karma.

stories.title: Purūravas and Urvaśī
stories.subtitle: A mortal king and an Apsaras argue at daybreak
stories.summary: Rigveda 10.95 is a dialogue hymn: Purūravas calls after Urvaśī; she answers that she is hard to hold. Later drama and Purāṇa expand this into a full romance; the hymn itself is a tense exchange.
stories.layerNote: Keep Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīyam and the Purāṇic romance distinct from the Rigvedic dialogue.

blocks.text: Like the Yama–Yamī hymn, this is a conversation preserved as a sukta, not a later stage play. A man calls to a woman who is leaving. The names Purūravas and Urvaśī are in the hymn; the later plot that explains why she leaves is not fully given here.
Purūravas asks her to stay and speak. {ref:RV.10.95.1}
Urvaśī answers that she has gone like the first of mornings; she is difficult to capture. {ref:RV.10.95.2}
The line later poets remember is already in the sukta.

The dialogue continues through a series of recriminations and refusals. Toward the end, talk of a son and of return appears in the hymn’s own words; this page does not fill the gaps from later narrative. {ref:RV.10.95.15} {ref:RV.10.95.18}

The full romance — the stolen lambs, the lightning, the son Āyu, the Gandharvas’ bargain, and Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīyam — is later narrative. The Rigvedic hymn is not automatically that story. Use 10.95 as the primary source, then read later versions as reception.

stories.title: Viśvāmitra and the Rivers
stories.subtitle: A seer asks two rivers to lower themselves for a crossing
stories.summary: Rigveda 3.33 addresses the Vipāś and Śutudrī. The rivers are speakers, not scenery. The hymn is a negotiation at the water’s edge.
stories.layerNote: Editorial narrative pointing to the dialogue hymn. Later epic stories of Viśvāmitra are not this sukta.

blocks.text: The hymn opens with the two rivers coming down from the mountains like mares loosed from the reins, like mothers licking a calf. {ref:RV.3.33.1} They are driven toward the ocean, each seeking the other. {ref:RV.3.33.2}

The human speaker — traditionally named Viśvāmitra in the anukramaṇī, and speaking in the hymn as one who comes with a wagon-train — addresses the most motherly river and asks, with sacred speech, for a crossing. {ref:RV.3.33.3} {ref:RV.3.33.5}

The rivers answer as speakers. They swell toward the ocean; they discuss whether they may stop for the Bharatas. The hymn is a negotiation, not a silent landscape. {ref:RV.3.33.4} {ref:RV.3.33.8} {ref:RV.3.33.10}
Later epic and Purāṇic cycles give Viśvāmitra a long career of rivalry, kingship, and ascetic power. Those stories are not Ṛgveda 3.33. This sukta is a river-crossing dialogue.

stories.title: Puruṣa Sūkta
stories.subtitle: A cosmic person is offered, and the world is said to arise
stories.summary: Rigveda 10.90 describes Puruṣa, a cosmic person of many heads and feet. The hymn says the world, the verses, animals, and human orders come from that offering. Later social uses of the hymn are a separate history.
stories.layerNote: Editorial narrative of the hymn. Later varṇa ideology and Purāṇic retellings are not silently merged into 10.90.

blocks.text: The Puruṣa Sūkta is a cosmogony in ritual language. It does not argue like the Nāsadīya. It describes a vast person and an offering from which parts of the world are named.

Puruṣa is said to have a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and to cover the earth on all sides, standing beyond it by ten fingers’ breadth. {ref:RV.10.90.1} All this is that Puruṣa: what has been and what will be. {ref:RV.10.90.2}
The gods, it says, offered Puruṣa as the oblation. From that sacrifice verses and chants are born, horses, cattle, goats and sheep. {ref:RV.10.90.6} {ref:RV.10.90.8} {ref:RV.10.90.9}

When they divided Puruṣa, the hymn asks, how many ways was he apportioned? The brāhmaṇa is his mouth; the rājanya is made of his arms; his thighs are the vaiśya; from his feet the śūdra is born. {ref:RV.10.90.11} {ref:RV.10.90.12}
The social classification is a claim inside this hymn. It is not a survey of all Vedic society, and it is not yet later dharmaśāstra.

The moon is born from the mind, the sun from the eye, Indra and Agni from the mouth, wind from the breath, atmosphere from the navel, sky from the head, earth from the feet. {ref:RV.10.90.13} {ref:RV.10.90.14}

One common scholarly observation is that 10.90 is linguistically and thematically late within the Rigveda, and that verse 12 became a charter text much later. That is an interpretation about history of use. The hymn still says what it says.

Later tradition recites this hymn widely and develops Puruṣa toward other cosmic persons and toward varṇa as a legal order. Those developments are real. They are not automatically the same as the Rigvedic sukta.

stories.title: Sarama and the Paṇis
stories.subtitle: A messenger and the keepers of hidden cows
stories.summary: Rigveda 10.108 is a dialogue: Sarama has crossed to the Paṇis and demands the cows. The Paṇis refuse and offer partnership. The hymn does not narrate the later full recovery story.
stories.layerNote: Keep later cow-recovery epics and the Rāmāyaṇa’s Śaramā distinct from this sukta.

blocks.text: This sukta is a conversation at a distance. The Paṇis have cows; Sarama has come. The hymn does not pause to explain the whole myth from outside. It lets the speakers question each other.
The Paṇis ask with what intention Sarama has come, for the way is far. {ref:RV.10.108.1} She answers that she has crossed the Rasā, sent as a seeker of the cows. {ref:RV.10.108.2}
Indra, she says, will take the cows; the Paṇis will not remain their keepers. {ref:RV.10.108.3} {ref:RV.10.108.5} They offer her partnership and cattle if she will stay. {ref:RV.10.108.7}
Sarama refuses to be a sister of the Paṇis or to divide the cows with them. She will go back; the cows will come out. {ref:RV.10.108.9} {ref:RV.10.108.10} {ref:RV.10.108.11}
The refusal is in the hymn. What happens after her return is not fully told here.

Later literature expands the Paṇi episode into a longer recovery of the cows, and a different Śaramā appears in the Rāmāyaṇa. Those are later stories. Ṛgveda 10.108 is the dialogue of arrival, demand, and refusal.

stories.title: Indra and the Release of the Waters
stories.subtitle: Hymns that name the slaying of the dragon and the release of waters
stories.summary: Several Rigvedic hymns praise Indra for slaying Vṛtra and releasing the waters. This page is an overview of those claims in the hymns, not a later Purāṇic biography of Indra.
stories.layerNote: Source-backed overview. Later epic Indra, Ahalyā, and the later Vṛtra cycle are not imported here.

blocks.text: The following verses keep action and landscape together: Indra drinks Soma, takes up the bolt, strikes the first-born of the dragons, and the obstructed waters move onward. {ref:RV.1.32.3} {ref:RV.1.32.4} {ref:RV.1.32.5}

The Rigveda does not keep the Indra–Vṛtra encounter in a single story-chapter. Poets return to it as a deed by which Indra is known: the dragon is slain, the waters move. This page follows two well-known hymns rather than assembling a later novel.
In Ṛgveda 1.32 the speaker will declare Indra’s manly deeds, the first that he achieved as wielder of the thunderbolt: he slew the dragon, then disclosed the waters. {ref:RV.1.32.1}
The hymn says the bolt was fashioned for him; he struck Vṛtra, who lay about the waters. {ref:RV.1.32.2} {ref:RV.1.32.11}
The opening of 1.32 states the deed without a later biography.

A different hymn, Ṛgveda 2.12, identifies Indra by a series of relative clauses. He is the one who made fast the shaking earth, who slew the dragon and freed the seven rivers. {ref:RV.2.12.1} {ref:RV.2.12.3}

Later epic and Purāṇic literature turns the encounter into fuller narratives about Indra, Vṛtra, and divine kingship. Those retellings belong to later tradition; this page stays with the Rigvedic hymns and their repeated image of waters released.

stories.title: The funeral hymn
stories.subtitle: Yama, the path of the departed, and the living who remain
stories.summary: Ṛgveda 10.14 addresses Yama and the fathers on the path of the dead. Nearby hymns speak to Agni at the pyre and tell Death to go a separate way. Later pretayāna manuals are a different literature.
stories.layerNote: Editorial guide to funeral suktas in maṇḍala 10. Not a handbook of later śrāddha.

blocks.text: Several hymns in the tenth maṇḍala speak at the edge of death. They are not one later funeral liturgy copied backward. Ṛgveda 10.14 is the central Yama hymn of this group; 10.16 and 10.18 are closely related.
The hymn honours Yama, Vivasvat’s son, who gathers men together. He went forth and found a way for many. {ref:RV.10.14.1} {ref:RV.10.14.2}
The departed is told to go forth along the ancient paths where the fathers have gone, and to meet Yama and Varuṇa. {ref:RV.10.14.7} {ref:RV.10.14.8}
Yama as finder of the path is a claim of this funeral hymn, not of the Yama–Yamī dialogue.
A neighbouring sukta addresses Agni with the body: do not burn him entirely; do not consume him; make him ripe for the fathers. {ref:RV.10.16.1}
Another neighbouring hymn tells Death to go its own way, apart from the path of the gods, and tells the living to turn back and dance. {ref:RV.10.18.1} {ref:RV.10.18.3}

Later tradition makes Yama a judge of karma and builds an elaborate geography of the dead. Ṛgveda 10.14 speaks of Yama, the fathers, and a path. It does not automatically contain that later system. The Yama of 10.10 is a speaker in a kinship dialogue, not simply the same figure as later Purāṇic Yama.

stories.title: The marriage hymn
stories.subtitle: Sūryā’s bridal, and verses later used in weddings
stories.summary: Ṛgveda 10.85 tells of Sūryā’s marriage. Later wedding ritual quotes parts of it. The later use is reception; the hymn’s own scene is the bridal of the sun-maiden.
stories.layerNote: Do not treat a modern wedding liturgy as if it were the Rigvedic narrative.

blocks.text: The long sukta 10.85 is the principal marriage hymn of the Rigveda. Its own story is celestial: Soma is bridegroom, Sūryā the bride. Human marriage appears as the hymn turns toward the home.
Truth is the base; Soma is placed in the sky. The hymn opens in that cosmic register. {ref:RV.10.85.1}
Sūryā’s bridal procession is described: the Aśvins are associated with the car, and the world is said to watch. {ref:RV.10.85.20}
Later the language turns to the taking of the hand and the hope of offspring and a household. {ref:RV.10.85.36} {ref:RV.10.85.42}
The taking of the hand is in the hymn. Later wedding books quote it; they do not replace it.

Gṛhya sūtras and later Hindu marriage rites reuse verses from 10.85. That later ritual history is important. It is not the same thing as reading the sukta as a hymn about Sūryā’s bridal. This page does not treat later custom as if it were already the Rigvedic plot.

stories.title: Hiraṇyagarbha
stories.subtitle: The golden embryo, and a refrain that keeps the god unnamed
stories.summary: Ṛgveda 10.121 praises the golden embryo as born in the beginning, lord of what is. A refrain asks to which god the offering should be made. Later identification with Brahmā is a different step.
stories.layerNote: Keep later Prajāpati–Brahmā cosmogonies labelled as later tradition.

blocks.text: This hymn does not proceed by the Nāsadīya’s unanswered questions, nor by the Puruṣa offering. It names a golden embryo (hiraṇyagarbha) born in the beginning, then keeps asking to which god the oblation belongs.
In the beginning arose Hiraṇyagarbha, born as the one lord of created being. He held up earth and heaven. {ref:RV.10.121.1}
The opening verse is the claim. The refrain that follows in the hymn keeps the addressee as a question.
The hymn continues: he who gives life and strength, whose command all beings follow, whose shadow is deathlessness and death. {ref:RV.10.121.2} {ref:RV.10.121.5}
The received hymn’s last verse addresses Prajāpati as the one who embraces all these created things. {ref:RV.10.121.10}

Some modern readers treat the Prajāpati closing as a later addition to a hymn whose refrain had left the god unnamed. That is a scholarly hypothesis about the text’s history. The received sukta still includes the verse.
Later tradition develops Hiraṇyagarbha toward a golden egg and toward Brahmā. Those cosmogonies are later literature. They should not be read silently into Ṛgveda 10.121.

stories.title: Agni at the Opening
stories.subtitle: The first hymn and the work of the ritual fire
stories.summary: The Rigveda opens by addressing Agni as priest, divine minister, and bearer of offerings. The hymn defines a relationship of daily approach rather than narrating a later birth-story of the fire god.
stories.layerNote: A guide to Rigveda 1.1. Later ritual systems and Purāṇic biographies are labelled separately.

blocks.text: The collection begins with an invocation rather than a creation story. Agni is addressed through the offices he performs between worshippers and gods.

The first verse calls Agni the household priest of the sacrifice, the divine officiant, and the bestower of treasure. {ref:RV.1.1.1} The next verses connect him with riches, offering, and access to the gods. {ref:RV.1.1.2} {ref:RV.1.1.3} {ref:RV.1.1.4}
The opening mantra establishes Agni by ritual function.
The singers approach Agni day by day, at night and dawn; the hymn closes by asking him to be accessible like a father to a son. {ref:RV.1.1.7} {ref:RV.1.1.8} {ref:RV.1.1.9}
Later ritual texts systematize multiple sacred fires, and later stories give Agni extended biographies. They illuminate reception but do not replace this compact opening address.

stories.title: Soma Flowing
stories.subtitle: Pressing, purification, exhilaration, and immortality
stories.summary: Soma is plant, pressed drink, flowing power, and deity in the Rigveda. These hymns praise its purification and effects without settling the modern botanical identity of the plant.
stories.layerNote: The botanical identity of Soma remains disputed; later identifications are not asserted as Rigvedic fact.

blocks.text: Maṇḍala 9 is organized around Soma Pavamāna — Soma while being purified and flowing. Its poetry repeatedly joins material pressing with divine agency.
Soma is urged to flow for Indra and the gods, purified through the filter and associated with strength and prize. {ref:RV.9.2.1} {ref:RV.9.2.3} {ref:RV.9.2.7} {ref:RV.9.2.10}
Read the opening of 9.2 as poetry of a substance in motion and a god addressed.
Elsewhere the drinkers say that they have drunk Soma and become immortal, while another hymn asks for the deathless realm of light. {ref:RV.8.48.3} {ref:RV.9.113.7}
Later traditions identify Soma with the moon and propose particular plants. Those histories are important but do not justify presenting one modern botanical candidate as certain.

stories.title: Uṣas, the Dawn
stories.subtitle: Radiance, awakening, and the measure of mortal days
stories.summary: The dawn hymns praise Uṣas as brilliant and life-awakening, yet each dawn also marks the passing of a mortal day.
stories.layerNote: A Rigvedic deity portrait; later goddess genealogies are not read backward into these hymns.

blocks.text: Uṣas is not merely a backdrop. The poets address dawn as a goddess whose recurring arrival reveals creatures, work, and time.
Her light appears and opens the way; she wakes living beings and makes paths visible. {ref:RV.1.113.1} {ref:RV.1.113.5} {ref:RV.7.75.5}
The opening verse places Dawn in a succession of light and darkness.
The same beauty measures human finitude: dawns have shone before and will shine after, while each appearance diminishes the span allotted to mortals. {ref:RV.1.113.10} {ref:RV.1.113.13}
Later literature places Uṣas in broader divine genealogies. Here the evidence is the dawn hymns themselves: praise intertwined with mortality.

stories.title: Varuṇa and the Bonds of Order
stories.subtitle: Cosmic watching, confession, and release
stories.summary: Varuṇa’s hymns join cosmic sovereignty with moral anxiety: the speaker asks what offence has been committed and seeks release from binding.
stories.layerNote: Later simplification of Varuṇa as only a water god is not projected onto the Rigvedic hymns.

blocks.text: Varuṇa is addressed as an all-seeing sovereign whose order encompasses the sky and human conduct. The poems also sound unusually personal.
The poet describes Varuṇa’s cosmic knowledge and asks that the upper, middle, and lower bonds be loosened. {ref:RV.1.24.10} {ref:RV.1.24.11} {ref:RV.1.24.15}
In 7.86 the speaker asks directly what offence has brought divine displeasure.

The inquiry becomes confession: inherited fault, wine, anger, dice, or heedlessness may lead a person astray; the prayer asks for freedom from that wrong. {ref:RV.7.86.3} {ref:RV.7.86.4} {ref:RV.7.86.5}
Later iconography and narrative frequently emphasize Varuṇa’s association with waters. That is later reception, not a reason to erase the sovereignty, bonds, and confession central here.

stories.title: Rudra in the Rigveda
stories.subtitle: Fierce, healing, and approached with careful praise
stories.summary: Rigveda 2.33 addresses Rudra as formidable and brilliant, asks that his weapons spare the community, and praises his healing remedies. Later Śiva theology is labelled as later reception.
stories.layerNote: Strictly Rigvedic portrait. Rudra’s later identification and development as Śiva is not treated as already complete in this hymn.

blocks.text: The hymn’s Rudra cannot be reduced either to wrath or to a later name of Śiva. Praise negotiates with a power who wounds and heals.
The singer seeks welfare for the household and asks Rudra not to strike children, adults, parents, or cattle. {ref:RV.2.33.1} {ref:RV.2.33.9} {ref:RV.2.33.10}
The praise calls Rudra the best physician of physicians and asks for his remedies.
The close again asks that the missile pass by and that healing medicines be granted. {ref:RV.2.33.14} {ref:RV.2.33.15}
Rudra becomes deeply identified with Śiva in later Vedic and post-Vedic tradition. That history should be stated, not used to import the entire later mythology into Rigveda 2.33.

stories.title: Vāc Speaks
stories.subtitle: A first-person hymn of speech and power
stories.summary: In Rigveda 10.125 the speaker identifies herself with divine powers, sustains gods and peoples, and declares the reach of her speech.
stories.layerNote: The first-person voice belongs to the hymn. Later goddess systems are reception, not silently substituted for it.

blocks.text: The poem is remarkable for its sustained first person. The speaker does not need an editorial narrator to grant her agency; the declarations are the structure of the hymn.
She moves with Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, and all gods, and bears Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Agni, and the Aśvins. {ref:RV.10.125.1}
The speaker names herself queen, gatherer of treasures, and first among those worthy of worship.

She says that the one she loves becomes powerful; she gives birth to the father on the world’s summit, and her greatness extends beyond earth and heaven. {ref:RV.10.125.5} {ref:RV.10.125.7} {ref:RV.10.125.8}
Later Śākta traditions read this hymn within developed goddess theology. That is a major reception history, distinct from describing only what this Rigvedic poem says.

stories.title: The Gambler and the Dice
stories.subtitle: Compulsion, loss, and an appeal to return home
stories.summary: The dice hymn speaks from inside gambling compulsion: exhilaration turns to debt, estrangement, and a final instruction to work the land instead.
stories.layerNote: Read as a Rigvedic poem of gambling and social damage, not as a modern clinical diagnosis.

blocks.text: The objects are small, but the poem makes them agents: brown dice from the vibhīdaka tree seize the speaker’s desire and reorder his household.

The gambler remembers their exhilaration, then describes a wife abandoned and a family that disowns him. {ref:RV.10.34.1} {ref:RV.10.34.3} The dice hook, burn, and overcome even the powerful. {ref:RV.10.34.7}
The poem’s practical turn tells the gambler: do not play with dice; cultivate the field.

The speaker sees another man at his wife’s side and spends the night in distress; at the end he addresses the dice themselves and asks for their favour or restraint. {ref:RV.10.34.10} {ref:RV.10.34.14}
The great dice games of the Mahābhārata are later narrative. They should not be treated as the plot of this first-person Rigvedic lament.

stories.title: The Frog Hymn
stories.subtitle: Voices after rain, heard beside ritual recitation
stories.summary: After a year of silence, rain awakens the frogs. The hymn compares their answering voices with students or priests reciting, mixing close observation and ritual wit.
stories.layerNote: The ritual comparison is in the hymn; a single allegorical key is not imposed on every detail.

blocks.text: The hymn watches an ordinary seasonal event with extraordinary attention: frogs reappear and call when the rains arrive.
Having lain silent for a year, the frogs raise their voices when the heavenly water reaches them, one answering another. {ref:RV.7.103.1} {ref:RV.7.103.2}
The opening announces the year-long silence and the return of voice.

Their alternating sounds are compared with pupils repeating a teacher and with priests around the Soma vessel. {ref:RV.7.103.6} {ref:RV.7.103.7} The closing asks the frogs for life and prosperity. {ref:RV.7.103.10}
Readers disagree over how satirical the priestly comparison is. The comparison itself is textual; its exact tone remains interpretive.

stories.title: Three Rigvedic Beginnings
stories.subtitle: Nāsadīya, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Puruṣa are not one account
stories.summary: Three famous hymns approach origin differently: unresolved inquiry, a golden embryo and repeated divine question, and a cosmic person offered in sacrifice.
stories.layerNote: Comparison preserves disagreement. It does not harmonize the hymns into one chronological creation story.

blocks.text: Calling all three hymns ‘creation myths’ can hide their strongest feature: they do not make the same claim or use the same poetic strategy.
The Nāsadīya begins before the ordinary opposition of being and non-being and ends by questioning whether even the highest overseer knows the origin. {ref:RV.10.129.1} {ref:RV.10.129.7}
Hiraṇyagarbha offers a different opening: a golden embryo arose in the beginning and upheld earth and heaven.

The received Hiraṇyagarbha hymn closes with Prajāpati. {ref:RV.10.121.10} The Puruṣa hymn instead makes sacrifice the generative action and maps social orders onto the cosmic body. {ref:RV.10.90.6} {ref:RV.10.90.12}
Later cosmologies can coordinate creator, cosmic egg, sacrifice, and metaphysical principles. This page resists treating that later synthesis as the original argument of each hymn.
